source: What Child Is This - We Voice (Part 1 of 2), Entry 2

blocks.text: 02: WHY DO WE CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS IN DECEMBER IF NOBODY KNOWS EXACTLY WHEN JESUS WAS BORN?

sentences: Every December, someone in the conversation brings it up.
Jesus wasn't really born on December 25th.
Nobody knows when He was born.
The whole thing is borrowed from pagan festivals anyway.
It gets said with the confidence of a person who has just neutralized the holiday, as if the uncertainty of the date unsettles the reality of the event.
It doesn't.
The date and the birth are two separate questions, and conflating them is one of the more common errors in Christmas-season conversation.
We don't know the exact date of the birth of Jesus.
That's true.
We also don't know the exact date of the birth of Julius Caesar, and no one uses that uncertainty to argue that Caesar wasn't born.

What we know about Christmas is exactly what an honest historical investigation can establish: a window of time, a location that has never been disputed, and a set of reasons for December that predate every pagan accusation aimed at it.
That's more than enough to work with, and it's where we need to start.

blocks.text: THE CALENDAR AND THE MONK WHO GOT IT WRONG

sentences: Before we can establish when Jesus was born, it helps to understand how we ended up with the calendar we use.
Most of us are familiar with BC and AD, and most of us assume that AD 1 marks the year Jesus was born.
That assumption is wrong, and the error is traceable to a specific person in a specific century.
In the first-century Roman world, the dating system in use was called the AUC system, which counted years from the traditional founding of the city of Rome.
Christians operating in that world used the same system.
It wasn't until 525 that Pope John I commissioned a monk named Dionysius Exiguus to develop a standardized calendar for the Western church.
Dionysius centered the new calendar on the birth of Jesus, designating that event as AD 1, the year of the Lord.
The concept of BC, counting backward from that point, didn't arrive until 731, when an English monk named Bede added that convention.
There's also no year zero in this system.
The calendar moves directly from 1 BC to AD 1, which creates minor arithmetic complications when doing ancient date calculations.
The problem is that Dionysius made a mistake.
Working with the historical records available to him in the sixth century, he placed the birth of Jesus four to six years later than the evidence now indicates it occurred.
This isn't a scandal.
It's simply what happens when a scholar in 525 works with incomplete data.
We've better data now, and the better data places the birth of Jesus not in AD 1 but somewhere in the window of 6 to 4 BC.
That construction, born in BC, sounds paradoxical to modern ears.
It isn't.
It simply means that the monk who created our calendar miscalculated, and the birth of Jesus predates the year the monk assigned to it.
The birth is the fixed point.
The calendar is the human attempt to organize time around it, and that attempt was slightly off.
Rather than chasing a specific date, the more useful approach is to establish the boundaries within which the birth had to occur.
The Biblical and historical record gives us two fixed points that function like bookends, and the birth of Jesus falls somewhere between them.
The later bookend is the death of Herod the Great.
Both Matthew and Luke place the birth of Jesus during the reign of Herod.
Matthew explicitly records that the Magi arrived in Jerusalem during his reign, and Luke opens the entire nativity sequence with a reference to Herod as the reigning king of Judea.
Herod the Great died in mid-March to mid-April of 4 BC.
That's the established historical consensus, derived from Josephus and corroborated by astronomical data matching the lunar eclipse Josephus records near the time of Herod's death.
Whatever else we may debate about the timing of the birth of Jesus, He can't have been born after the death of the king the gospels say was on the throne when He arrived.
The later bookend is 4 BC.
The earlier bookend comes from Herod himself.
When the Magi failed to report back to him, Herod ordered the killing of all male children in Bethlehem two years old and under, calibrating the age range to the time he had learned from the Magi.
That two-year window implies that the birth of Jesus occurred no more than roughly two years before Herod issued the order.
Working backward from Herod's death in 4 BC, the earlier boundary lands around 6 BC.
The birth of Jesus, on the best available historical evidence, occurred between 6 and 4 BC.
Bethlehem as the location has never been seriously contested by any scholar, hostile or otherwise.
That's the historical conclusion: a real birth, a real place, a datable window of approximately two years in which it occurred.

Now we can address the date more specifically, because the accusation that December 25th was borrowed from pagan festivals is one of the most confidently repeated claims about Christmas and one of the least accurate.

The accusation goes like this: the early church, looking to compete with Roman festivals like Saturnalia or the birth of the sun god, strategically placed Christmas in December to absorb existing celebrations into the Christian calendar.
It sounds plausible.
It has been repeated so many times that most people treat it as settled history.
The problem is that it doesn't hold up under examination.
The Roman festival of Saturnalia wasn't celebrated in 6 to 4 BC, the window in which Jesus was born.

The Persian worship of Mithras, another common target of this accusation, wasn't a significant presence in the Roman Empire until well into the second century AD, long after Christmas was being observed.
The timeline doesn't work.
The Christian observance predates the pagan competition it's alleged to have copied.
The actual origin of December 25th is considerably less dramatic and considerably more interesting.
The earliest Christians held a belief that great prophets died on the same date they were conceived.
This idea, sometimes called the integral age tradition, led them to conclude that Jesus was conceived on March 25th, the date they believed He died.
Nine months from March 25th is December 25th.
That calculation is where the date comes from.
It has nothing to do with Saturnalia and nothing to do with Mithras.
It comes from an early Christian theological conviction about the symmetry of the life of a prophet.
Whether that theological reasoning is correct is a separate question.
It doesn't need to be correct to be historically significant.
What it establishes is that the earliest Christians had a specific reason, rooted in their own theological framework, for observing the birth of Jesus in December.
That reason predates the accusations aimed at it.
The charge that Christmas was invented to compete with pagan holidays requires us to ignore the evidence that explains December 25th without any reference to paganism at all.

blocks.text: THE METHODOLOGY THAT CARRIES US FORWARD

sentences: There's a principle in all of this that will serve us through the rest of this book, and it's worth naming plainly.
In historical investigation, we work from what we can establish toward what we can't.
We don't demand perfect certainty before we accept a historical conclusion, because perfect certainty isn't the standard applied to any other ancient event.

We accept that Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon, that Alexander the Great conquered Persia, and that the eruption of Vesuvius buried Pompeii, all without demanding a level of documentation we don't apply to the Christmas story.

What we can establish about Christmas is this: a historical figure whose existence is attested by hostile external sources was born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great, in a window of time that the evidence places between 6 and 4 BC.
The December date reflects an early Christian tradition with its own internal logic and no dependence on pagan precedent.
The calendar we use to mark December 25th was set by a monk who made a modest arithmetic error, which is why the year we assign to it doesn't match the historical evidence for when it occurred.
None of that uncertainty touches the event itself.
The uncertainty is about precision.
The event isn't in question.
Christmas isn't a date.
Christmas is a birth.
The date is our best attempt to honor it.
The birth is a fact.
We routinely accept historical events without knowing their exact dates.
What standard are we actually applying when we use the uncertainty of December 25th to question the reality of the birth itself?
The pagan festival accusation against Christmas requires the Christian observance to be later than the pagan festivals it supposedly copied.
The evidence shows the opposite.
How do we account for the persistence of a claim that doesn't survive a basic timeline check?
Dionysius made a calculation error in 525 that affected the entire Western calendar, and yet the event he was trying to date was real enough to organize a calendar around.
What does it tell us about the significance of the birth of Jesus that even an imperfect attempt to center history on it reshaped how the entire world marks time?
